chinese_fuxi.name: Institute the rites of marriage
chinese_fuxi.notes: Credited with regulating marriage and the giving of betrothal gifts (a pair of deerskins), establishing the institution of the family.

chinese_fuxi.name: Replace knotted cords with the first written signs
chinese_fuxi.notes: In the Xici commentary to the Yijing, Fuxi devised written tallies and the trigrams to replace government by knotted cords.

chinese_guanyin.name: Manifest a thousand arms and eyes
chinese_guanyin.notes: The thousand-armed, thousand-eyed form arises from her vow to aid all beings at once; each hand bears a saving implement and an eye of compassion.

chinese_houyi.name: Receive the elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West
chinese_houyi.notes: Granted the pill (or twin pills) of deathlessness by Xiwangmu after his labors; the elixir Chang'e then took to the moon.

chinese_gun.name: Dam and dyke the floodwaters
chinese_gun.notes: Attempted to halt the Great Flood by piling up barriers with the self-swelling soil over nine years; the containment strategy failed where his son Yu's dredging succeeded.

chinese_huangdi.name: Gaze on the four quarters with four faces
chinese_huangdi.notes: Tradition (cited in the Shizi and discussed in the Taiping Yulan) gives the Yellow Emperor four faces, by which he watched over all four directions of his realm at once.

chinese_huangdi.name: Defeat Chiyou at Zhuolu
chinese_huangdi.notes: Overcame the rebel Chiyou in the fog-bound battle of Zhuolu, aided by the south-pointing chariot and the drought-spirit Ba.

sources.reference: Sima Qian, Shiji, 'Annals of the Five Emperors'

chinese_yao.name: Order the calendar and the seasons
chinese_yao.notes: Commissioned the Xi and He astronomer-officials to observe sun, moon and stars and to fix the seasons and the intercalary year.

chinese_yao.name: Yield the throne to the worthy
chinese_yao.notes: Passed the sovereignty to the commoner Shun after testing rather than to his own son Danzhu, the founding model of merit-based succession.

chinese_yu_the_great.name: Tame the Great Flood by dredging the channels
chinese_yu_the_great.notes: Succeeded where his father Gun failed by cutting drainage channels to lead the waters to the sea, laboring thirteen years and passing his own door three times without entering.

chinese_yu_the_great.name: Divide the land into the Nine Provinces
chinese_yu_the_great.notes: After draining the floods he surveyed and apportioned the realm into nine provinces with graded tribute.

chinese_houji.name: Make the hundred grains flourish
chinese_houji.notes: As a child he delighted in planting beans, gourds, hemp and grain that grew abundantly; appointed Minister of Agriculture, he taught the people sowing and reaping.

chinese_leizu.name: Discover the rearing of silkworms and the reeling of silk
chinese_leizu.notes: Discovered that the cocoon unwinds into thread and taught silkworm husbandry, reeling and weaving; honored as patron of sericulture.

chinese_sun_wukong.name: Wield superhuman strength
chinese_sun_wukong.notes: Born of stone, he hefts the 13,500-jin iron pillar as a weapon and battles the hosts of Heaven single-handed.

sources.reference: Wu Cheng'en, Xiyouji (Journey to the West)

chinese_zao_jun.name: Ascend yearly to report the household to Heaven
chinese_zao_jun.notes: On the 23rd/24th of the twelfth month he rises to the Jade Emperor to report each family's conduct, by which their fortune for the coming year is set.

sources.reference: Baopuzi (Ge Hong), 'Weizhi' / Kitchen God folk tradition

chinese_ehuang.name: Preside as a goddess of the Xiang River
chinese_ehuang.notes: After drowning in grief she became, with her sister, a tutelary spirit of the Xiang; invoked as Xiang Jun / Xiang Furen in the Chuci 'Nine Songs'.

sources.reference: Chuci, 'Jiuge' (Nine Songs): Xiang Jun, Xiang Furen

chinese_nuying.name: Preside as a goddess of the Xiang River
chinese_nuying.notes: Together with her elder sister Ehuang she became a deity of the Xiang after drowning in sorrow, the consort-goddesses addressed in the Chuci.

chukchi_kurkil.name: Bring fire, water and the useful arts to mankind
chukchi_kurkil.notes: In the Beringian Raven cycle Kurkil/Kutkh gives humankind fire, fresh water, speech and skills such as net-making.

sources.reference: Bogoras, Chukchee Mythology (Jesup North Pacific Expedition)

chuukese_olifat.name: Arm the sharks with teeth
chuukese_olifat.notes: A malicious culture-act: Olifat gave the sharks their teeth so that they would bite humans, one of the harms attributed to him.

sources.reference: Lessa, Tales from Ulithi Atoll (Iolofath cycle)

chuukese_olifat.name: Be born from his mother's head
chuukese_olifat.notes: Sprang from the head of Tarisso and at once fled, refusing human touch, cleaning himself on palm trunks and biting through his own cord.

chuukese_anulap.name: Teach humankind wisdom, law and craft
chuukese_anulap.notes: As the high creator-spirit Anulap is the source of knowledge and the magical and practical arts handed down through his son Lugeilan.

chuukese_lugeilan.name: Mediate between the sky-gods and mankind
chuukese_lugeilan.notes: Called 'Middle of Heaven', he is lord over spirits and mortals and the channel by which his father Anulap's gifts reach humanity.

sources.reference: Soushenji (In Search of the Sacred); standard Shennong tradition

sources.reference: Shennong Bencaojing (Han compilation attributed to Shennong)

chinese_jade_emperor.name: Birthday of the Jade Emperor (Tian Gong Dan)
chinese_jade_emperor.cadence: annual, ninth day of the first lunar month
chinese_jade_emperor.notes: Households and temples (especially in Taiwan and Fujian) light lanterns, burn incense, and offer sugarcane, rice cakes and theatrical performances to the Lord of Heaven.

sources.reference: Chinese New Year folk-ritual ethnography; temple practice in Taiwan/Fujian

chinese_zao_jun.name: Sending-off of the Kitchen God
chinese_zao_jun.cadence: annual, 23rd/24th day of the twelfth lunar month
chinese_zao_jun.notes: On the 'Little New Year' the family burns the old stove-portrait to send Zao Jun to Heaven, smearing sticky malt-sugar on his lips so his report will be sweet; a new image is pasted up at New Year.

sources.reference: Chinese New Year folk-ritual ethnography (the 'little new year' / xiaonian)

chinese_houji.name: Sacrifice at the Altars of Soil and Grain
chinese_houji.notes: As patron of grain Houji received offerings at the she-ji altars, the 'soil-and-grain' shrines that became a metonym for the state itself.

sources.reference: Liji (Book of Rites); Zhou state-altar practice

chinese_shennong.name: Sacrifice at the Mausoleum of the Yan Emperor
chinese_shennong.notes: As ancestor-god of farming and medicine, Shennong (Yandi) receives ancestral sacrifice at the Yandi Mausoleum in Yanling, Hunan, a rite listed as national intangible cultural heritage.

sources.reference: Yandi Mausoleum sacrificial ceremony (PRC national intangible cultural heritage)

chinese_leizu.name: Cult of the Silkworm Mother
chinese_leizu.cadence: seasonal, at the start of sericulture
chinese_leizu.notes: Identified with the Silkworm Mother (Canmu / Can Nainai), Leizu receives village offerings for healthy silkworms and successful spring rearing, sometimes through a spirit-medium.

sources.reference: Silkworm-Mother village cult (Hebei field study); Canshen tradition

chinese_yu_the_great.name: Great Sacrifice to Yu at Kuaiji
chinese_yu_the_great.notes: Yu's mausoleum, temple and ancestral hall stand at Kuaiji (Shaoxing); the sacrifice, revived as a national ceremony in 'monarchical form', honors the flood-tamer and dynastic founder.

sources.reference: Ritual Ceremony for Great Yu at Kuaiji (Zhejiang); cult of Yu tradition

chinese_houyi.name: Moon-altar offering (later Mid-Autumn observance)
chinese_houyi.cadence: associated with the eighth-month full moon
chinese_houyi.notes: In the Chang'e legend Houyi sets out his wife's favorite fruits and incense before the moon, an offering folk tradition links to the Mid-Autumn Festival.

chinese_yaoji.name: Worship at the Divine Maiden Temple, Mount Wu
chinese_yaoji.notes: A temple to the Wushan goddess stood by the Yangtze gorges; in Daoist canonization she bears the title Miaoyong Zhenren.

sources.reference: Wushan Shennü temple tradition; Daoist title Miaoyong Zhenren

chinese_erlang_shen.name: Erlang worship at Guankou
chinese_erlang_shen.notes: Worshipped at Guankou (Dujiangyan) in Sichuan as a river-taming and flood-controlling deity; farmers prayed at his temples by canals and weirs for protection from flood.

chukchi_dawn.name: Sacrifice to the Dawn quarter
chukchi_dawn.notes: Chukchi tents face Morning-Dawn, the pre-eminent benevolent Being; the principal animal sacrifices (reindeer among herders, dog among maritime Chukchi) are directed to the Dawn, with a fox sent down in exchange for the sacrificed dog.

sources.reference: Bogoras, The Chukchee (Jesup North Pacific Expedition)

chukchi_midday.name: Sacrifice to the Mid-day quarter
chukchi_midday.notes: Mid-day, with Dawn, receives the greater share of the directional sacrifices among the benevolent Beings (taaronyo vairgit).

sources.reference: Bogoras, The Chukchee (Jesup North Pacific Expedition)

chukchi_zenith.name: Sacrifice to the Zenith (Middle-Crown)
chukchi_zenith.notes: The Zenith-being is chief of the benevolent Beings sacrificed to; offerings are directed upward to the 'middle-crown' at the apex of the sky.

sources.reference: Bogoras, The Chukchee (Jesup North Pacific Expedition)

chuukese_inemes.name: Love-magic invocation of Inemes
chuukese_inemes.cadence: as needed, for love and desire
chuukese_inemes.notes: Inemes is the goddess imprecated in Chuukese love-magic spells and love-potions, and she descends upon a spirit-medium in the lineage meeting-house.

sources.reference: Bollig, Die Bewohner der Truk-Inseln (1927); Micronesian Seminar, spirit possession in Chuuk

attributes.name: Human upper body with a serpent's tail
attributes.notes: In Han tomb art Fuxi has a human head and torso above a coiling serpentine (dragon) tail, his tail entwined with Nüwa's.

sources.reference: Han tomb reliefs, Nanyang (Henan); Wu Liang shrine carvings

attributes.name: Holds the carpenter's square (ju)
attributes.notes: He bears the set-square that draws the square Earth, the complement to Nüwa's compass; the pair codify cosmic geometry.

sacredAnimals.name: Dragon (his serpentine body and his clan's dragon-naming of offices)

attributes.name: Human upper body with a serpent's tail
attributes.notes: Depicted as a beautiful woman above, serpent (dragon) below; with Fuxi their tails interlace like a double helix, signifying their creative union.

sources.reference: Han tomb reliefs, Nanyang; Wu Liang shrine

attributes.name: Holds the compasses (gui)
attributes.notes: She bears the pair of compasses that draw the circle of Heaven, complement to Fuxi's set-square.

sources.reference: Han tomb iconography of the serpent-bodied creator pair

attributes.name: Ox head on a human body
attributes.notes: Shown with the head (or horns) of an ox, recalling the plough-ox and his role as Divine Farmer.

attributes.name: Transparent abdomen
attributes.notes: A see-through stomach by which he watched how each tasted herb and its toxin acted within him.

sources.reference: Shennong 'First Emperor of the Five Grains' tradition

attributes.name: Flowing white robe (Baiyi Guanyin)
attributes.notes: In China most often a serene woman in a white robe, the White-Robed Guanyin.

attributes.name: Eleven heads above a thousand arms
attributes.notes: Esoteric form combining the eleven-headed and thousand-armed manifestations, each hand with an eye and a saving implement.

attributes.name: Standing on a dragon or a lotus
attributes.notes: Frequently shown atop a sea-dragon or a lotus, attended by the boy Shancai and the Dragon-Girl Longnü.

sources.reference: Chinese Guanyin iconography; Sudhana and Longnü acolyte tradition

attributes.name: Tiger's teeth and panther's tail (early form)
attributes.notes: In the Shanhaijing she has wild hair, tiger's fangs and a leopard's tail, dwelling in a cave and whistling; later strata refine her into a stately queen.

sources.reference: Shanhaijing, 'Xishan jing' (Classic of the Western Mountains)

attributes.name: Enthroned with the sheng headdress and three attendant creatures
attributes.notes: In Han art she sits in her sheng head-ornament attended by a three-legged crow, a jade hare pounding the elixir, a nine-tailed fox, and the three blue/green birds that fetch her food.

sources.reference: Han iconography of Xiwangmu (mirrors, tomb reliefs)

attributes.name: Hairy, horned giant clad in leaves or bearskin
attributes.notes: Portrayed as a primordial giant covered in hair (or bearskin and leaves) with horns on his head, grasping axe and chisel, or the sun and moon.

sources.reference: Pangu iconographic tradition; Birrell, Chinese Mythology

sacredAnimals.name: The four numinous creatures: dragon, qilin, phoenix and turtle

sources.reference: Pangu iconography (accompanied by the four spiritual animals)

attributes.name: Human (copper/iron) head with red hair on a serpent's body
attributes.notes: A humanoid head, sometimes copper-faced and iron-browed, with vivid red hair, set on the long body of a black serpent-dragon.

sources.reference: Gonggong iconographic tradition; Werner, Myths and Legends of China

attributes.name: Blue-bodied beast with bat-wings, beak and talons
attributes.notes: A fearsome figure with a blue body, bat-like wings, bird's beak, three eyes and clawed feet, bare-torsoed in a crimson loincloth, beating a ring of drums.

sources.reference: Lei Gong iconography (Dunhuang Mogao Cave 285; Song and later depictions)
Wei-period and Dunhuang depictions of the half-bird thunder-being

attributes.name: Man-faced beast riding a pair of dragons
attributes.notes: In the Shanhaijing the fire-god has a man's face on a beast's body and rides two dragons; he governs fire, summer and the south.

attributes.name: Seated in imperial dragon-robe and tasselled crown, holding the jade tablet
attributes.notes: Enthroned as a bearded sovereign in the long dragon-embroidered robe and mianguan crown of strung jade beads, holding the gui audience-tablet, exactly as a Chinese emperor.

sources.reference: Daoist iconography of the Jade Emperor

attributes.name: Associated with the Yellow Dragon and ascent on a dragon
attributes.notes: His emblematic animal-form is the Yellow Dragon; at his death a dragon descended and bore him up to Heaven, his ministers clinging to its whiskers.

sources.reference: Sima Qian, Shiji, 'Treatise on the Feng and Shan Sacrifices'

attributes.name: Vertical truth-seeing third eye on the forehead
attributes.notes: His signature feature is a third, vertical eye in the middle of the brow that pierces all disguise; shown as an armored young warrior with his three-pointed lance and the celestial hound at his side.

sources.reference: Erlang Shen iconographic tradition; Xiyouji and Fengshen yanyi

attributes.name: Youthful child-warrior in lotus-petal garb
attributes.notes: Depicted as a boy reborn from lotus root and flesh, riding the Wind-Fire Wheels, the Universe Ring on his arm and the Red Armillary Sash about his shoulders, the fire-tipped spear in hand.

attributes.name: Robed, capped official depicted with his wife on the stove-portrait
attributes.notes: Shown as a bearded man in official's robes and scholar's cap, paired with his wife, in the paper poster pasted above the kitchen stove.

sources.reference: Kitchen God print tradition; Werner, Myths and Legends of China

attributes.name: Scholar in robe and 'pure-yang' turban, sword across his back
attributes.notes: Portrayed as a handsome bearded scholar in flowing robe and the chunyang turban, the demon-quelling Pure-Yang sword slung at his back and a horsehair fly-whisk in hand.

sacredAnimals.name: The ten sun-crows (three-legged crows he shot down)

sacredPlants.name: Spotted (mottled) bamboo, stained by the sisters' tears
Spotted (mottled) bamboo, stained by the sisters' tears

attributes.name: Octopus form
attributes.notes: Hit is the octopus sea-goddess whose ribald dance made the sky-wife Hamulul faint, allowing Olifat's conception.

sources.reference: Bollig, Die Bewohner der Truk-Inseln (1927); Olifat conception cycle
